findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementors
findings.body: CryptoProvider.order() is added as a plain abstract method (no default implementation). CryptoProvider is a public, SPI-loaded extension point (discovered via META-INF/services and ServiceLoader in CryptoIntegration). Any existing third-party or downstream implementation of this interface that is not updated to implement order() will fail to compile/load. Since this interface is explicitly designed for pluggable crypto backends (FIPS vs non-FIPS, custom providers), this is a breaking API change that should either provide a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 100; }`) or be clearly called out as a breaking change in release notes.

findings.title: Removed fail-fast check for multiple CryptoProviders now silently resolves ties non-deterministically
findings.body: Previously, detecting more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath threw an IllegalStateException, which protected against misconfiguration (e.g. accidentally shipping both a FIPS and non-FIPS crypto module together). Now, detectProvider() just sorts by order() and silently keeps the first. All of DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider return the same order() value of 200, so if two of them ever end up on the same classpath/classloader, the choice between them depends on the arbitrary ServiceLoader iteration order (not guaranteed to be stable across JVMs/OS), rather than failing loudly. In a FIPS-mandated deployment this could silently select the non-FIPS provider instead of raising an error, which is a meaningful loss of a safety net with potential compliance/security consequences.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return a BouncyCastle provider, violating the documented contract
findings.body: CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented as returning 'BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider'. This implementation instead returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is whatever JCA provider backs the JVM's default keystore type (typically the JDK's built-in SUN provider), completely unrelated to BouncyCastle. Other providers that don't rely on BouncyCastle (e.g. WildFlyElytronProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()) simply return null, which is the established convention for 'no BC provider'. Returning an arbitrary unrelated Provider instance here is inconsistent with that convention and can mislead any code that relies on this method's contract (e.g. diagnostics, provider registration logic) if this CryptoProvider instance is ever the active one.

findings.title: Dead code: throwaway ASN1Encoder instances created and discarded
findings.body: In concatenatedRSToASN1DER(), two ASN1Encoder instances are created and `write()` is called on them, but the results are never used or assigned (lines 114-115); the actual return value is built via separate, freshly-created ASN1Encoder instances a few lines later. This is leftover/dead code from development that performs unnecessary object allocation and encoding work on every signature conversion call, and should be removed before merging.

findings.title: ES384/ES512 tests reuse a single default-curve EC key, never exercising real signature lengths for those algorithms
findings.body: The single EC KeyPair used across all three tests (testES256/testES384/testES512) is generated with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` without specifying a curve, which defaults to a 256-bit curve (e.g. secp256r1/P-256) regardless of the algorithm under test. For ES384 and ES512 the real R/S components should be ~48 and ~66 bytes respectively, but because the same P-256 key is reused, the actual signature always has ~32-byte components that get zero-padded to the expected length in asn1derToConcatenatedRS/concatenatedRSToASN1DER. As a result, the tests never exercise the encoder/decoder with genuinely large R/S values (e.g. values requiring a leading 0x00 byte near the boundary of a 48- or 66-byte field), reducing their ability to catch boundary bugs specific to the larger curves these algorithms are meant to represent.
